title.en: Describe loans from commercial banks and financial institutions

say.en: A company can borrow from thousands of people at once by issuing debentures. Why might it prefer this to issuing more shares? In this lesson: Explain debentures and their types.
Describe loans from commercial banks and financial institutions.
Explain public deposits.

body.en: A debenture is an acknowledgement of a debt by a company. Debenture holders are creditors, not owners: they get interest at a fixed rate whether or not the company earns profit, and have no voting rights. Interest is a charge on profit and is tax-deductible, so debt is cheaper than equity. *Debentures* may be secured or unsecured, registered or bearer, convertible or non-convertible, and first or second.
body.kn: ಸಾಲಪತ್ರದಾರರು ನಿಗದಿತ ಬಡ್ಡಿ ಪಡೆಯುವ ಸಾಲಗಾರರು. ಬಡ್ಡಿ ತೆರಿಗೆ ಕಡಿತಾರ್ಹವಾದ್ದರಿಂದ ಸಾಲಪತ್ರಗಳು ಷೇರುಗಳಿಗಿಂತ ಅಗ್ಗದ ಮೂಲ.

title.en: Banks, financial institutions and public deposits

body.en: Commercial banks give loans and advances, cash credit, overdraft and discounting of bills, mainly for short and medium term; they usually ask for security. *Financial institutions* such as IFCI, ICICI, IDBI, SIDBI and the State Financial Corporations provide medium and long-term finance and are also called development banks; they also give technical and managerial advice. Public deposits are deposits raised directly from the public by companies, usually for up to three years, at a rate higher than bank deposits.
body.kn: ಬ್ಯಾಂಕುಗಳು ಮುಖ್ಯವಾಗಿ ಅಲ್ಪ ಮತ್ತು ಮಧ್ಯಮಾವಧಿ ಸಾಲ ನೀಡುತ್ತವೆ, ಅಭಿವೃದ್ಧಿ ಬ್ಯಾಂಕುಗಳು ದೀರ್ಘಾವಧಿ ಹಣಕಾಸು ನೀಡುತ್ತವೆ, ಕಂಪನಿಗಳು ಸಾರ್ವಜನಿಕರಿಂದ ನೇರವಾಗಿ ಠೇವಣಿಯನ್ನೂ ಪಡೆಯಬಹುದು.

problem.en: A company needs ₹10,00,000 and expects earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) of ₹2,00,000. Tax rate is 30%. Plan A: issue 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10. Plan B: issue 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 and ₹5,00,000 of 10% debentures. Compare earnings per share (EPS).

steps.en: Plan B: interest = 10% × 5,00,000 = ₹50,000; profit before tax = ₹1,50,000.
Return on investment (20%) is more than the interest rate (10%), so using debentures raises EPS: this is trading on equity.

answer.en: EPS is ₹1.40 under Plan A and ₹2.10 under Plan B; debt raises the return to equity shareholders.

narration.en: Let us work through this together. A company needs ₹10,00,000 and expects earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) of ₹2,00,000. Tax rate is 30%. Plan A: issue 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10. Plan B: issue 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 and ₹5,00,000 of 10% debentures. Compare earnings per share (EPS).

say.en: Let us work through this together. A company needs 10,00,000 rupees and expects earnings before interest and tax EBIT of 2,00,000 rupees. Tax rate is 30 percent. Plan A: issue 1,00,000 equity shares of 10 rupees. Plan B: issue 50,000 equity shares of 10 rupees and 5,00,000 rupees of 10 percent debentures. Compare earnings per share EPS.
Plan A: no interest; tax equals 30 percent times 2,00,000 equals 60,000 rupees; profit after tax equals 1,40,000 rupees; EPS equals 1,40,000 divided by 1,00,000 equals 1.40 rupees.
Plan B: interest equals 10 percent times 5,00,000 equals 50,000 rupees; profit before tax equals 1,50,000 rupees.
Tax equals 30 percent times 1,50,000 equals 45,000 rupees; profit after tax equals 1,05,000 rupees; EPS equals 1,05,000 divided by 50,000 equals 2.10 rupees.
Return on investment 20 percent is more than the interest rate 10 percent, so using debentures raises EPS: this is trading on equity.
So the answer is EPS is 1.40 rupees under Plan A and 2.10 rupees under Plan B; debt raises the return to equity shareholders.
